overview.text: Operation BREAKTHROUGH is a HUD research and development program to modernize the housing industry and demonstrate industrialized housing systems on nine prototype sites across eight areas of the nation, including Indianapolis, Jersey City, Kalamazoo, Macon, Memphis, Sacramento, St. Louis, Seattle, and King County, Washington. HUD considered alternatives such as no program, a purely technological program, varying the number and character of demonstration sites, and limiting demonstrations to a single housing system per site, but rejected them in favor of the broader demonstration approach. Potential environmental impacts include changes in storm runoff, visual effects of land use change, impacts on community services, and noise, with site-specific mitigations such as earthen berms, holding basins, and a siphon system, plus a total energy plant at Jersey City projected to use about half the fuel of conventional alternatives. Federal agencies including EPA, Interior, Agriculture, and FPC submitted comments, with EPA requesting separate impact statements for each site and Agriculture warning about repeating past land-use mistakes.

project_description.text: Operation BREAKTHROUGH is a HUD research and development program to modernize the housing industry and bring about volume production of industrialized housing through demonstration of innovative housing systems on nine prototype sites in eight areas of the nation. Specific program activities include demonstrations of new building materials and methods, total energy systems, and pneumatic trash collection, with twenty-two housing systems selected. The total energy installation at Jersey City is intended to provide heating, air conditioning, and domestic hot water, with construction proceeding across multiple sites.

affected_community.text: The nine prototype sites span eight areas including Indianapolis, Jersey City, Kalamazoo, Macon, Memphis, Sacramento, St. Louis, Seattle, and King County, Washington. Site characteristics range from central city urban renewal properties to suburban neighborhoods, providing housing opportunities for a wide range of income levels. Specific sites address local concerns such as overcrowded schools in Jersey City and noise from major roadways in Memphis.

alternatives_overview.text: Four alternatives were considered: no program, a program directed only at housing technology, different number and character of demonstration sites, and a different site design philosophy such as one system per site. The 'no program' option was rejected because the housing problem is too critical, and a purely technological program was deemed unable to overcome institutional constraints. Additional technological alternatives included conventional electrical service versus total energy systems and the emerging fuel cell technology, which Pratt and Whitney did not recommend for current demonstration use.

environmental_impact.text: Potential adverse impacts include changes in storm runoff, visual effects of land use change, impacts on community services, and possible effects on local property values. Site-specific mitigations include earthen berms for noise at Memphis, holding basins to reduce flooding at Indianapolis, and a siphon system to prevent eutrophication of the Macon lake. The total energy plant at Jersey City is projected to use about half the fuel of conventional alternatives with lower thermal and air pollution, and HUD has adopted noise abatement policies prohibiting support to new construction on sites with unacceptable noise exposures.

public_response.text: Comments were received from EPA, Interior, HEW, Agriculture, Army, Transportation, Commerce, FPC, and HUD offices. EPA requested more detail on air pollution impacts and basic information about activities at each location. Interior raised concerns about psychological effects of mass housing, while Agriculture warned about repeating past land-use mistakes. DOT found the statement acceptable, and FPC noted that total energy systems are not new.

value.name: No Program
value.description: The option of not implementing Operation BREAKTHROUGH at all. This alternative was never seriously considered given the critical nature of the national housing problem.

evidence.quote: No Program

value.name: Program Directed Only at Housing Technology
value.description: A program limited solely to developing new housing technologies, without addressing the constraints and barriers to innovation. This was rejected because technology alone, without tackling implementation obstacles, would have little chance of widespread adoption.

evidence.quote: Program Directed Only at Housing Technology

value.name: Different Number and Character of Demonstration Sites
value.description: Varying approaches to the types and number of demonstration sites were considered, ranging from a 'housing fair' with one example of each housing system to using only federal land. The chosen approach required demonstrating both housing and community development across a wide range of situations.

evidence.quote: Different Number and Character of Demonstration Sites

value.name: Different Site Design Philosophy
value.description: An approach that would limit each demonstration site to a single housing system, allowing that system to showcase many different housing types. This was rejected in favor of exposing all selected systems as broadly as possible given budget, site design, and marketing considerations.

evidence.quote: Different Site Design Philosophy
